summary:
At the lunar south pole, the Sun rises only about 1.5° above the mean horizon and Earth about 1°. A ridge can determine whether a lander has sunlight, a direct-to-Earth link, both or neither. RAVEN helps planners, students and educators compare lunar sites through a unified web app.

The RAVEN Mission Planner combines scenario comparison with the eight-stage RAVEN Engine: JPL DE440 ephemerides NASA LRO LOLA terrain, and models of solar illumination, battery state of charge, radio-link margin with diffraction, and Deep Space Network visibility. It presents mission-feasibility verdicts and visualizations in Learning and Advanced modes.

RAVEN SI provides a locally hosted, citation-grounded assistant for explanations and mission planning. The RAVEN Prediction Model adds neural surrogates and sensor-fusion estimators, with human review before models are
promoted.

RAVEN is an open-source learning and planning tool. Licensed under Apache-2.0
details:
RAVEN is a web-based decision-support and learning tool that helps planners compare lunar south-pole landing sites and mission windows.

Its eight-stage engine combines JPL DE440 ephemerides with NASA LRO LOLA terrain to estimate solar visibility and power, battery charge, direct-to-Earth radio-link margin, including terrain diffraction and Deep Space Network visibility, then presents comparable results and feasibility verdicts.

The goal is to make fragmented technical data easier to explore. We support better-informed early mission trade-offs and engage students and educators, without claiming flight qualification.

We built it as a modular full-stack app using Svelte 5 and Typescript, Python 3.12+ with FastAPI and Three.js/WebGL with a Canvas 2D fallback. It also includes a locally hosted, citation-grounded RAVEN SI assistant and ONNX-based predictive estimators, with human review for model promotion.

RAVEN is creative in bringing terrain, energy, communications, and interactive 3D into one workflow. The design considers harsh polar lighting, ridge blockage, energy reserves, uncertainty, accessibility, and offline use on standard computers.
